title: Does Weak-to-strong Generalization Happen under Spurious Correlations?
claim: Spurious group structure and differing pre-trained representations of teacher and student are modeled as latent signal plus group features with differing encoding efficiency.
layout: Left-to-right, three rows of arrows linking toy example to matrix diagrams, annotation callouts
description: A dense theory-setup diagram. At top left, a blue box poses a cow-vs-camel classification task with a Gaussian latent model for z(x) and label y. Arrows lead down to cartoon camel and cow icons, then to red minority/majority group boxes (Pr[g=1]=η, Pr[g=0]=1−η) over desert and grassland background images. A pink box defines the group feature ξ(x). The middle column has three wide arrows, in blue, orange and green. They show that the weak teacher and strong student share z(x), the teacher encodes ξ(x) less efficiently, and the student encodes it more efficiently. Each arrow carries Stiefel-manifold notation. The right side shows grey matrix blocks for the teacher and student feature maps, with colored z(x), tensor-product and φ segments. Gray callouts hold dimension inequalities and the teacher-student similarity Ξ = TᵀS. The eye goes first to the blue task box, then to the colored arrows.

abstract: We initiate a unified theoretical and algorithmic study of a key problem in weak-to-strong (W2S) generalization: when fine-tuning a strong pre-trained student with pseudolabels from a weaker teacher on a downstream task with spurious correlations, does W2S happen, and how to improve it upon failures? We consider two sources of spurious correlations caused by group imbalance: (i) a weak teacher fine-tuned on group-imbalanced labeled data with a minority group of fraction $Î·_\ell$, and (ii) a group-imbalanced unlabeled set pseudolabeled by the teacher with a minority group of fraction $Î·_u$. Theoretically, a precise characterization of W2S gain at the proportional asymptotic limit shows that W2S always happens with sufficient pseudolabels when $Î·_u = Î·_\ell$ but may fail when $Î·_u \ne Î·_\ell$, where W2S gain diminishes as $(Î·_u - Î·_\ell)^2$ increases. Our theory is corroborated by extensive experiments on various spurious correlation benchmarks and teacher-student pairs. To boost W2S performance upon failures, we further propose a simple, effective algorithmic remedy that retrains the strong student on its high-confidence data subset after W2S fine-tuning. Our algorithm is group-label-free and achieves consistent, substantial improvements over vanilla W2S fine-tuning.
